notes.meaning: Sarah lived to be 127 years old. Scripture honors her by recording her age, death, and burial, which it does for no other woman in the Bible. Her long life had seen God faithfully keep His promise of giving her a son.

Sarah died in Hebron, in the land of Canaan where she had traveled for many years. Abraham mourned deeply and wept for the loss of his beloved wife. His tears showed real affection and honor for her memory, while still trusting in God.

After sitting in sorrow, Abraham stood up to arrange Sarah's burial. Attending to this duty kept his grief from overwhelming him completely. He approached the local Hittite leaders at the city gate to ask for help.

Abraham spoke of himself as a foreigner and an outsider who owned no ground in Canaan. He asked to buy a burial site so he could lay Sarah to rest with dignity. Even though God had promised him the whole land, Abraham still lived as a humble traveler.

The Hittites answered Abraham with great respect, calling him a leader blessed by God. They offered him the choice of their best burial places free of charge. Their generous words showed that they recognized God's favor in Abraham's life.

Abraham stood up and bowed before the Hittites to thank them for their kindness. Religion teaches believers to show good manners and honor to those in authority. Abraham remained polite and humble even while planning to decline their offer.

Abraham asked the leaders to speak with a man named Ephron about purchasing the cave of Machpelah. The cave lay at the end of Ephron's field, and Abraham insisted on paying full price for it. He wanted a permanent family tomb of his own in the land God had promised.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation renders Machpelah as the 'double cave,' following an ancient tradition that the burial place had two chambers or parts.

notes.meaning: Ephron was sitting among the citizens at the city gate where public business took place. He offered to give Abraham both the field and the cave without charging him anything. This was a courteous Eastern way to show goodwill and open the negotiation.

Abraham bowed again before the people and politely insisted on paying for the land. He refused to take it as a gift so that he would not take advantage of Ephron's kindness. Paying full value also ensured that his family's legal right to the tomb would never be challenged.

Ephron replied by naming a price of four hundred shekels of silver, while adding that such an amount meant little between friends. He named the value openly so the sale could move forward without awkwardness. His words kept the conversation polite and friendly.

Abraham agreed to the price and weighed out the four hundred shekels of silver in front of everyone. In those days, silver was weighed out by standard amounts used by traders rather than in coins. Abraham paid the entire sum right away, showing fairness and honesty in his business.

The field, the cave, and every tree within its borders were legally transferred to Abraham. This agreement was made publicly before all the citizens at the city gate. Doing business openly in front of witnesses gave Abraham a secure and unquestioned title.

Once the land was legally his, Abraham buried Sarah in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron. This cave later became the resting place of Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob. Burying Sarah in Canaan proved Abraham's faith that God would fulfill His promise to give that land to his family.

The field and its cave were fully confirmed as Abraham's permanent property for a burial place. This grave was the only piece of the promised land that Abraham ever owned while he lived. Securing it showed his trust in God's promises and his expectation of the resurrection.
